author: Kate Sharpley
title: We Have Fed You All for a Thousand Years : Travels of a Protest Poem
content:
As ‘We Have Fed You All for a Thousand Years’ this poem is possibly the most widely reprinted item from Freedom.

In September 1893 the London anarchist newspaper Freedom : A Journal of Anarchist Communism published a poem called ‘A Humble Reminder : To the Propertied Classes’, credited to ‘N.’[1] It’s an anti-capitalist protest, lamenting the ‘workers’ dead’ whose deaths enriched those ‘propertied classes’. It rails at the rich ‘We have fed you all for a thousand years, / And you hail us still unfed’. I do not know who ‘N.’ was, though they seem to be connected to the Freedom milieu. Freedom had published another poem by them, ‘The Pet Voter’, in August 1892.[2] Max Nettlau used the same initial when writing in Freedom in June 1891; the Fabian socialist Edith Nesbit had a poem ‘A Word For The Children’ in Freedom in February 1891 (‘The right to give help is your own, / The right to claim it theirs.’) Neither seems a convincing candidate for the authorship of this poem. The Kipling connection

‘N.’ introduced their poem by saying it was ‘slightly altered from Rudyard Kipling’s Ode in praise of English Enterprise.’ That’s a reference to Kipling’s ‘Song of the Dead’ published four months earlier in The English Illustrated Magazine (May 1893). ‘N.’s address to the propertied classes ‘For if blood be the price of England’s wealth, / Good God, we ha’ paid in full’ rewrites Kipling’s address to the sea ‘If blood be the price of admiralty, / Lord God, we ha’ paid in full!’.[3] The ‘Humble Reminder’ changes Kipling’s poem – but leans heavily upon it. Mark Leier said ‘strictly speaking the poem is not a parody of Kipling’s poem but a re-working of the words based on the original verse and meter.’[4] It reminds me of Utah Philips’ comment on IWW songmaking: ‘The Wobblies liked to steal the hymn tunes ‘cos they were pretty and change the words so they made more sense.’[5]

The connection to Kipling persisted. He was credited in many of the reprints (inevitable, perhaps, given that the author remained unknown and their debt to Kipling was clear). There were even articles discussing what it would mean if the poem were by Kipling.[6] Reprinted and recited

Once printed, it was always possible for the poem to reappear, and this one spread beyond the anarchist press, becoming a standard of labour movement papers. The title often changed, varying from ‘The Cry of Toil’ to ‘The Capitalist’. Just as the connection to Kipling is sometimes there and sometimes not, the text varies between the poetic ‘ha’’ to the everyday ‘have’.

Apparently a version was published in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania in 1895.[7] The Portland anarchist newspaper The Firebrand reprinted the poem (anonymously) as ‘The Workers Outcry’ in 1897.[8] Changes had been made to Americanise the text: instead of pounds the third line talks of ‘there’s never a dollar of all your wealth’.

Sometimes you can read about the poem’s life off the printed page. In May 1897 Miss Olive Keep recited ‘We have fed you all for a thousand years’ at a gathering of the Socialist Labor Party. [9]. In August 1899, The Carpenter, a union journal for ‘Carpenters, Stair Builders, Machine Wood Workers, Planing Mill Men, and Kindred Interests’ reprinted the ‘Firebrand version’ (with credit).[10] In 1904 the poem reappeared as ‘The Price of England’s Wealth’ in Glasgow’s The Voice of Labour.[11] This version talks of ‘sovereigns’ rather than ‘pounds’ or ‘dollars’ but there are other changes: I can’t tell if it’s rewritten from the Freedom or Firebrand version.

The anarchist journal Mother Earth (‘published every 15th of the month’) reprinted ‘The Cry of Toil’ (credited to Kipling) in April 1908.[12] On April 18, 1908 it appeared in the IWW’s Industrial Union Bulletin (also credited to Kipling).[13] Once the poem was reprinted in the IWW songbook, and was later put to music (‘about 1916’ by Rudolf von Liebich), it was firmly established as a classic of working class protest.

In November 1913 strikers in Auckland used a line from the poem on their banner during the 1913 Waterfront Strike: ‘If blood be the price of your cursed wealth, good God we have bought it fair’.[14] It’s not often we get the names of people who helped circulate the text but ‘Gordon’ suggested it (as ‘The Workers’ Answer’) in the 1917 compilation New songs for Butte Mining Camp.[15]

As ‘We Have Fed You All for a Thousand Years’ this poem is possibly the most widely reprinted item from Freedom. In March 1969 it was reprinted (from the IWW songbook, credited to an ‘unknown proletarian’) on the front of the third issue of the Bulletin of the Anarchist Black Cross. The band Palm Ghosts released a version in August 2026. Questions remain: Who was N? How did it get into Mother Earth? If anyone sees any evidence, please let us know. Notes

author: Marx-lover
title: The Cornell Case and the Left's Betrayal of Itself
content:
Here's an article about the feminist reaction to the "Cornell 7" case that has been in the news recently (October 2026). A version of it was published in "Compact." (The hyperlinks have been deleted, unfortunately.) The general point is that contemporary feminism has become an albatross for the left, and is also contributing to destructive social and cultural trends.

In the 1960s, feminists demanded that women and men have legal equality, that women be treated as mature adults who are free to make their own choices be it with regard to sex or their careers, that patriarchal paternalism be dismantled. In the 2020s, feminists demand that women be constantly protected against men, that patriarchal paternalism be resurrected, that women be legally treated as not responsible for decisions they’ve made because, in certain contexts, only men have agency. And men, they argue, are inveterate misogynists, abusers, and rapists, so the agency they manifest is almost invariably malign.

The reaction to the “Cornell 7” case is the latest example. A remarkable wave of hysteria has swept liberal and left culture, from mass media and social media to university campuses. Misandry is drenching the discourse; mobs are going after anyone who questions the dominant narrative; the guilt of the accused is automatically assumed, because the accused are men and men are by definition guilty. author: 张皓翔
title: The Dislocation of Vendémiaire (IV): The Misrecognized Socialism and the Resisters Who Refuse Connection 【葡月的错位（四）被误认的社会主义与拒绝联结的抗争者】 【A commentary on the French riots between September and October】
content:
This essay is the fourth part of The Dislocation of Vendémiaire. Drawing on Karl Marx's famous "sack of potatoes" metaphor from 1851, it contrasts the historical inability of the French peasantry to unite with the contemporary resisters of the 2026 French/European movements who actively "refuse connection." The author argues that while previous struggles centered on physiological survival, modern struggles have shifted to the realm of existential subjectivity—the refusal to be treated as mere interchangeable parts ("elementalization") within social machinery. The essay re-examines the Soviet experience, arguing that it substituted market-based elementalization with a planned one, thereby creating a historical illusion that alienated modern resisters from political organizations. Ultimately, the text critiques the movement's decentralized, anti-party stance as "eating the child with the bathwater," arguing that without the vanguard, organization, and discipline, resisting a highly organized capitalist state machine is impossible.

author: rezgar2
title: تجدید سازمانی چپ در عصر دیجیتال
content:
پنهان نیست که چپ در بسیاری از کشورهای جهان در سال های اخیر شاهد افول بوده است. دلایل زیادی برای این افول وجود دارد، چه عینی و چه ذهنی، اما ساختار سازمانی و اشکال کار و رهبری نقش بزرگی در آن داشته اند. بنابراین معتقدم این مرحله نیازمند تغییر تدریجی از ساختار سلسله مراتبی به ساختار افقی است، جایی که پایه، نسل های جدید و زنان بیشترین نقش را در شکل دهی سیاست ها و انتخاب رهبران دارند و رهبری از پایگاه حمایت می کند، از آن حمایت می کند و کار آن را هماهنگ می کند. این مفاهیم از مجموعه ای از تجربیات چپ در کشورهای مختلف بهره می برند. این مفاهیم مفید و روشنگر هستند، اما به کارگیری آن ها نیازمند سازگاری دقیق است که ویژگی خاص هر جامعه و شرایط پیچیده آن را در نظر می گیرد و نمی توان آن ها را به سادگی منتقل کرد. با این حال، نیروهای چپ در هر جامعه ای بازتابی از سطح توسعه آن در دانش، حقوق و دموکراسی باقی می مانند و انتظار می رود که در خط مقدم آن توسعه و نیروی محرکه آن باشند. این همان چیزی است که نوسازی سازوکارهای سازمانی آن ها را در جنوب جهانی و غرب به یک ضرورت فوری تبدیل می کند. یادگیری در اینجا در هر دو جهت جریان دارد، زیرا تجربیات چپ در جنوب جهانی، با تمام آنچه از کار و سازماندهی تحت سرکوب دارد، به نوبه خود چیزی برای ارائه به چپ در کشورهای پیشرفته دارد. جایی که شروع کردم به پایان می رسم. حزبی که دموکراسی، عدالت، شفافیت و رهبری جمعی را در ساختار خود به کار می گیرد، به زنان و مردانی که با دست و مغز کار می کنند، شواهد عملی از توانایی خود در اجرای این ارزش ها در اداره دولت و جامعه ارائه می دهد.

author: Kate Sharpley
title: Barry Pateman: An Appreciation
content:
It’s important to appreciate those who have come before us. I first met Barry through Albert Meltzer, probably at a bookfair. I’d learned to trust that if Albert thought well of someone, he was probably right.

Barry was an impressive man, physically and mentally, with the sort of self-deprecating humour instantly recognisable to anyone brought up in a British working class environment. And he was able to talk to people, without the sort of academic language that can be so off-putting.

The times I saw him were few and far between but they were always memorable. Barry was brimming with ideas, whether about anarchist history, theory and practice, sport or wider culture. Like Albert he had a high regard for the autodidacts – especially those miner militants whose self-education far outstripped those who had had a university education. He was good company.

It was perhaps telling that I learned of Barry’s death a few days after returning from Ron Marsden’s funeral. Both had been intimately involved in the tension between organising as anarchists and remaining accessible to ordinary people.
